panel.finding_key: packages/sheets/src/model/worksheet/format.ts::sheets date formatter does not recognise the new timestamptz raw text form (`2025-06-15 05:30:00+00`) that query cells now carry
panel.summary: Sheets date formatter does not recognise the new TIMESTAMPTZ raw text form (`2025-06-15 05:30:00+00`) that query cells now carry
panel.evidence: packages/sheets/src/model/worksheet/format.ts:24-66 recognises only `YYYY-MM-DD` and `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS`; anything else falls through to `new Date(value)` with `hasTime: false` (:62-66), which drops the time component on render. Previously TIMESTAMPTZ arrived as a JS Date and was serialised to an ISO 'Z' string; with the new raw-text parser it arrives as `2025-06-15 05:30:00+00`, matching neither regex. Only bites when a date number-format is applied to a query-result cell, hence medium confidence.

coderabbit.summary: The `MONEY` assertion is locale-dependent and may fail on non-US clusters.
coderabbit.evidence:
_🎯 Functional Correctness_ | _🟡 Minor_

<details>
<summary>🧩 Analysis chain</summary>

🌐 Web query:

`In PostgreSQL, is the textual output of the `money` type controlled by the database or cluster locale setting such as `lc_monetary`?`

💡 Result:

In PostgreSQL, the textual output of the money data type is indeed controlled by the locale setting, specifically the lc_monetary configuration parameter [1][2]. Key points regarding this behavior include: 1. Locale Dependency: The output format (such as currency symbols, decimal separators, and digit grouping) depends on the active setting of lc_monetary [1][3]. Because the textual representation is locale-sensitive, it is important to ensure that lc_monetary remains consistent when moving or restoring data between databases [1]. 2. Configuration Scope: The lc_monetary parameter can be set at the cluster level (in postgresql.conf), the database level, or changed on-the-fly for a specific user session or transaction using the SET command [2][3]. 3. Fractional Precision: In addition to the display format, the fixed fractional precision used by the money type is also determined by the database's lc_monetary setting [1]. Because of this dependency on the client or session locale, applications should be aware that the same money value may appear differently depending on the environment in which it is queried [1][3].

Citations:

- 1: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-money.html
- 2: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/locale.html
- 3: https://dba.stackexchange.com/questions/183964/is-it-possible-to-insert-un-formatted-data-for-money-data-type-in-postgresql

---



</details>

**The `MONEY` assertion is locale-dependent and may fail on non-US clusters.**

PostgreSQL formats the `money` type using the database's `lc_monetary` setting, which dictates the currency symbol and digit grouping. Since the test asserts the exact string `$1,234.56`, it will fail on databases configured with different locales.

Either set `lc_monetary` to `en_US.UTF-8` in the test setup or avoid asserting the formatted string output.

<details>
<summary>🤖 Prompt for AI Agents</summary>

```
Verify each finding against current code. Fix only still-valid issues, skip the

In `@packages/backend/test/database.e2e-spec.ts` around lines 244 - 245, The MONEY
expectation in the database e2e spec is locale-dependent because PostgreSQL
formats money using lc_monetary, so the exact string asserted in the
type-mapping table can fail on non-US setups. Update the money-related assertion
in the database test to either explicitly set lc_monetary to en_US.UTF-8 in the
test setup before running the query, or relax the assertion so it does not
depend on the formatted currency string; use the existing MONEY/MACADDR mapping
in the e2e spec to locate the case.
```
